{"id": "68:8/q01", "question": "How does the opening fa connect this prohibition to what precedes?", "turns_on": "Which preceding consideration the command is drawn from: the sura's praise and assurances, the guided-versus-astray contrast, or the prospect of divine justice.", "positions": [{"id": "68:8/q01/p1", "position": "The preceding assurances and praise of the Prophet lead to this practical command.", "reasons": "Alusi allows the whole preceding sura as the ground. Elmalılı calls the fa consequential and the first practical result of the earlier assurances, opening counsel for the mission. Ibn Ashur says the praise of the Prophet and his guidance prepares the transition. Razi contrasts the accusation of madness with his religious and moral excellence, and says the command steels him despite his few supporters and the deniers' many. Ibn Kathir grounds it in God's gift of upright law and magnificent character. Bint al-Shati says the opening affirms his mission and steadies him against those calling the Qur'an ancient tales and disputing its miraculous nature."}, {"id": "68:8/q01/p2", "position": "The command follows specifically because the Prophet is guided while the deniers are astray.", "reasons": "Alusi gives this as one possible antecedent of the consequential fa. Ibn Ashur grounds it in 68:7 and says he should answer their hostility to truth firmly. Tabatabai likewise derives the prohibition from their error."}, {"id": "68:8/q01/p3", "position": "The prospect that God's wisdom and justice will appear calls for ignoring the deniers of resurrection.", "reasons": "Islahi says those deniers suppose they would retain their present favors even if resurrection came."}]}
{"id": "68:8/q02", "question": "What does 'obey' mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether iṭāʿah here is compliance with requests, conciliatory conduct, or susceptibility to influence; Alusi expressly offers conciliation in place of literal obedience.", "positions": [{"id": "68:8/q02/p1", "position": "Accepting requested action or compliance, including agreement in speech or deed.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur defines obedience as accepting an action someone seeks and says the negation bars every kind of compliance with their requests. Tabatabai explicitly includes agreement in speech or action. Elmalılı renders the demand as not heeding, obeying, or following their false path."}, {"id": "68:8/q02/p2", "position": "Conciliation or gentleness toward the deniers, including outward compromise against conviction.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur explains the word here as conciliation and gentleness and compares 25:52. Alusi reports the possibility that the target is ingratiating compromise, outwardly displaying what conflicts with the Prophet's conviction to win their hearts, rather than literal obedience."}, {"id": "68:8/q02/p3", "position": "Being affected or influenced by them.", "reasons": "Islahi says this use of iṭāʿah occurs in both Qur'anic and classical Arabic."}]}
{"id": "68:8/q03", "question": "Who are 'the deniers'?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase identifies the Meccan opponents, a particular clan, deniers by the truth they reject, or specifically deniers of resurrection.", "positions": [{"id": "68:8/q03/p1", "position": "The Meccan polytheists or Quraysh leaders who approached the Prophet.", "reasons": "Wahidi al-Basit and Razi call them Meccan leaders; Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, and the Study Quran identify Meccan polytheists or disbelievers. Ibn Atiyya names Quraysh. Qurtubi reports this identification. Their invitations are detailed under the question about the proposal."}, {"id": "68:8/q03/p2", "position": "People who deny God's oneness, revelation, signs, truth, or the Messenger's prophethood.", "reasons": "Tabrisi specifies denial of oneness and prophethood; Abu Hayyan, denial of God's revelation; Bint al-Shati, rejection of God's signs and the Messenger's prophethood. Kur'an Yolu describes those calling him a liar and denying truth. Ibn Ashur identifies denial of his mission."}, {"id": "68:8/q03/p3", "position": "The Banu al-Mughira, including named members of that clan.", "reasons": "Muqatil says the verse was revealed concerning the clan, including al-Walid, Abu Qays, and Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayya, as well as other named members."}, {"id": "68:8/q03/p4", "position": "Deniers of resurrection who assume they would retain their favors if it came.", "reasons": "Islahi specifies their denial and their expectation about their favors."}]}
{"id": "68:8/q04", "question": "Why does the verse call them 'deniers'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:8/q04/p1", "position": "Their denial itself explains why they must not be obeyed.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says the designation points to their denial of the Prophet's mission as the reason for the prohibition. Al-Malwi, as reported by Biqa'i, says denial corrupts the intellectual and speaking faculties and is the root of every unbelief, deviation, innovation, and evil."}]}
{"id": "68:8/q05", "question": "What did the deniers ask the Prophet to do?", "turns_on": "The terms of the proposed bargain: adoption of their ancestral faith, alternating worship, or reciprocal cessation of opposition.", "positions": [{"id": "68:8/q05/p1", "position": "Follow their religion or venerate their idols, often specified as the ancestral Meccan religion.", "reasons": "Muqatil says they called him to his fathers' religion and community and cites 25:52. Wahidi al-Basit and Wahidi al-Wajiz say they invited him to their religion. Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Razi, Qurtubi, and the Study Quran specify the religion of their forefathers; Qurtubi calls it corrupt, and the Study Quran says they urged his followers too, instead of revelation. Abu Hayyan mentions invitations to venerate idols."}, {"id": "68:8/q05/p2", "position": "Alternate worship of God and their deities as a bargain.", "reasons": "Kashshaf and Nasafi say they proposed worshipping God for a time and their idols for a time, in exchange for leaving the Prophet unharmed. Ibn Atiyya describes Quraysh proposing reciprocal worship of one another's deities. Nasafi also separately states the alternating worship and protection terms."}, {"id": "68:8/q05/p3", "position": "End mutual opposition while each side keeps its worship.", "reasons": "Qurtubi says the polytheists offered to stop opposing him if he stopped opposing them. Ibn Ashur says they offered to stop calling him mad if he stopped humiliating their idols and forebears, leaving each side to worship as it wished; he relates the offer to the warnings of 68:5–7 and 68:51. He also reports that sira books say the offer was conveyed through Abu Talib and Utba ibn Rabi'a."}]}
{"id": "68:8/q06", "question": "What conduct does the prohibition require?", "turns_on": "Whether the command emphasizes refusal of religious demands, avoidance of outward conciliation, or disregarding resurrection deniers in view of divine justice.", "positions": [{"id": "68:8/q06/p1", "position": "The Prophet must refuse the deniers' religious demands and stand firm against compromise.", "reasons": "Muqatil, both Wahidi works, Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Razi, Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan, and the Study Quran describe refusal of their ancestral religion or idolatrous requests. Tabrisi extends refusal to requests from those denying oneness and prophethood. Kashshaf, Baydawi, Nasafi, Alusi, and Razi stress firm resistance; Nasafi and Kashshaf specify the alternating-worship offer. Qurtubi says accommodation would be disbelief. Ibn Kathir grounds refusal in upright law and excellent character. Elmalılı calls for persistence in the mission amid injustice and rebellion. Ibn Ashur says to answer their hostility to truth firmly and allow no form of compliance. Tabatabai includes agreement in speech or act. Kur'an Yolu says not to yield or slacken because God's path is right and truth cannot be mixed with falsehood."}, {"id": "68:8/q06/p2", "position": "He should avoid ingratiating compromise, even an outward show contrary to his conviction.", "reasons": "Alusi reports this as another possibility for the force of the prohibition, aimed at winning their hearts rather than literal obedience. Ibn Ashur reads obedience here as conciliation and gentleness."}, {"id": "68:8/q06/p3", "position": "He should ignore the deniers of resurrection in trust that God's wisdom and justice will become manifest.", "reasons": "Islahi says those deniers imagine they would enjoy the same favors even at resurrection."}]}
{"id": "68:8/q07", "question": "Who receives the command through its address to Muhammad?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:8/q07/p1", "position": "The Prophet is directly addressed, and the lesson extends to his community or other people.", "reasons": "Biqa'i says Muhammad is addressed but his community is intended, especially under persecution that could tempt even a sensible person to compromise. Elmalılı extends the admonition to all rational people. Kur'an Yolu says all believers are addressed through the Prophet."}]}
{"id": "68:8/q08", "question": "What limit does this command put on forbearance and generosity?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:8/q08/p1", "position": "They are virtues only when they do not promote injustice or compromise.", "reasons": "Elmalılı says true generosity lies in purity, sincerity, courage, and patiently teaching their outcomes."}]}
{"id": "68:8/q09", "question": "What is reported about the verse's revelation or the approach to the Prophet?", "turns_on": "The notes supply different kinds of setting detail: the clan concerned, the intermediaries in the offer, and its early timing.", "positions": [{"id": "68:8/q09/p1", "position": "It was revealed concerning the Banu al-Mughira.", "reasons": "Muqatil names al-Walid, Abu Qays, Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayya, and other members of the clan."}, {"id": "68:8/q09/p2", "position": "The offer was carried through Abu Talib and Utba ibn Rabi'a.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur attributes this report to sira books

{"id": "68:8/q11", "question": "What inward aim follows from refusing the deniers?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:8/q11/p1", "position": "The believer's aim and witnessed goal should be one because the worshiped One is one.", "reasons": "Qushayri derives unity of aim from the oneness of the One worshiped."}]}
{"id": "68:9/q01", "question": "What does waddū say about the opponents' wish?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:9/q01/p1", "position": "They loved or wished for an accommodation that they actually proposed.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says a merely private wish would not explain the command against obeying them; their offer was conveyed to the Prophet."}]}
{"id": "68:9/q02", "question": "How does law tudhinu function after waddū?", "turns_on": "Whether law voices an unattained wish, retains a conditional apodosis, or acts as a verbal noun particle.", "positions": [{"id": "68:9/q02/p1", "position": "Law expresses a wish, 'if only you would compromise.'", "reasons": "Al-Burhān compares 11:80, 2:167, and 39:58. Bursevī calls it optative; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says it conveys a remote, frustrated wish and reports the comparison with layta."}, {"id": "68:9/q02/p2", "position": "Law remains conditional, with an unspoken object of waddū and an unspoken answer to law.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān attributes this to most grammarians; al-Samīn prefers 'they wished for your accommodation; had you done so, they would have rejoiced.' Al-Ālūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr also supply an omitted consequence."}, {"id": "68:9/q02/p3", "position": "Law can serve as a verbal noun particle like an: they wished for his accommodation.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān attributes this to Basrans; Ibn ʿĀshūr names al-Farrāʾ, al-Fārisī, al-Tabrīzī and Ibn Mālik. Al-Itqān reports this construal for the reading without nūn."}]}
{"id": "68:9/q03", "question": "What does tudhinu or idhān mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the oil metaphor denotes ordinary softness or specifically deceptive religious laxity.", "positions": [{"id": "68:9/q03/p1", "position": "It means softening, lenience, accommodation or ingratiating speech and conduct.", "reasons": "Al-Layth and Abū al-Haytham stress gentle speech; al-Farrāʾ and al-Mubarrad's discussants specify softness toward someone undeserving. Al-Ṭabarī, al-Jushumī, al-Biqāʿī, Bursevī, Ibn ʿĀshūr and Bint al-Shāṭiʾ derive the figurative softness from oil. Al-Māwardī and al-Qurṭubī cite poetry about accommodating an enemy; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ notes literal oil in 23:20 and 55:37 and figurative usage in 56:81; al-Wāḥidī also points to 56:81."}, {"id": "68:9/q03/p2", "position": "It can mean dissembling: concealing hostility, betraying religion, or abandoning sincere counsel.", "reasons": "Al-Mufaḍḍal gives hypocrisy and lost counsel; al-Mubarrad says one outwardly shows the opposite of one's inward stance. Al-Jawharī and al-Jushumī distinguish dāhana, concealment, from adhana, cheating. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ gives evasive appeasement and laxity as related senses; Ibn Barrajān speaks of knowing neglect of truth."}, {"id": "68:9/q03/p3", "position": "The related verb can mean demeaning, denying, or taking something lightly.", "reasons": "Study Quran gives these additional senses without supporting argument."}]}
{"id": "68:9/q04", "question": "What did the opponents want the Prophet to do?", "turns_on": "Whether 'softening' names a reciprocal concession generally or a specific act: idolatry, silence, disbelief, deception, abandonment, lying or weakness.", "positions": [{"id": "68:9/q04/p1", "position": "Make mutual concessions or soften his stance in religion.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, al-Kalbī, al-Ḥasan and many others describe a bargain; al-Rāzī specifies abandoning some commitments. Al-Ṭabarī reports Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda. Asad and Kur'an Yolu extend it to ethical and spiritual principles. Al-Qurṭubī accepts the listed glosses as compatible applications of softness, against Ibn al-ʿArabī's narrowing."}, {"id": "68:9/q04/p2", "position": "Disbelieve, allowing or confirming their own disbelief.", "reasons": "Reports from Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, ʿAṭiyya, al-Suddī and others repeat this. Al-Wāḥidī treats it as a form of concession; Ibn al-ʿArabī calls disbelief or lying strongest, while al-Qurṭubī rejects narrowing the verse to these."}, {"id": "68:9/q04/p3", "position": "Incline toward their idols and leave the truth.", "reasons": "Mujāhid is repeatedly cited. Al-Ṭabarī prefers this and cites 17:75; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reports his preference and cites 17:74. Al-Wāḥidī calls it the majority view and links al-Wālibī's report from Ibn ʿAbbās."}, {"id": "68:9/q04/p4", "position": "Take turns worshipping their idols and God.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba's proposed exchange is repeated by al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Qurṭubī and Kur'an Yolu. Al-Biqāʿī relates the year-for-year proposal to the occasion of Sūrat al-Kāfirūn (109:1)."}, {"id": "68:9/q04/p5", "position": "Stop denouncing idolatry, unbelief, sins or their forebears, letting each side practice its religion.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās adds that such softness corrupts religion; al-Bayḍāwī mentions ceasing to forbid shirk or sometimes agreeing to it. Al-Biqāʿī and Ibn ʿĀshūr specify idols and ancestors. The latter links their offer to accusations in 68:5–7 and 68:51; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ reports 'leave him and his Lord alone.'"}, {"id": "68:9/q04/p6", "position": "Dissemble or display piety outwardly while concealing the opposite.", "reasons": "Zayd ibn Aslam gives reciprocal hypocrisy; al-Ālūsī clarifies that the opponents wanted only outward softness from the Prophet, since they would dislike his inward dissent. Bursevī warns that outward compliance without inward conviction is fleeting hypocrisy."}, {"id": "68:9/q04/p7", "position": "Abandon the religious mission altogether.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī, al-Qurṭubī and Abū Ḥayyān transmit this from Qatāda."}, {"id": "68:9/q04/p8", "position": "Lie, so that they could lie too.", "reasons": "Attributed to al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas; Ibn al-ʿArabī considers lying, alongside disbelief, among the strongest glosses."}, {"id": "68:9/q04/p9", "position": "Weaken or relent, allowing them to do likewise.", "reasons": "Attributed to Abū Jaʿfar by al-Māwardī, al-Qurṭubī and Abū Ḥayyān."}]}
{"id": "68:9/q05", "question": "What would the opponents do in return?", "turns_on": "What particular concession or conduct the preceding idhān names, and whether their response is promised or already being performed.", "positions": [{"id": "68:9/q05/p1", "position": "Reciprocate by softening, accommodating or making concessions.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba speaks of each religion; al-Kalbī says each party would leave what the other dislikes. Al-Bayḍāwī says they defer their own accommodation until the Prophet acts; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ says the wish covers both clauses."}, {"id": "68:9/q05/p2", "position": "Continue or join in disbelief.", "reasons": "The repeated reports say his disbelief would license or confirm their own; Study Quran states that they want believers to become disbelievers too."}, {"id": "68:9/q05/p3", "position": "Worship God in an alternating exchange with idol worship.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba's formulation varies between an unspecified period and a year in al-Biqāʿī's report; Kur'an Yolu and Study Quran repeat the proposed exchange."}, {"id": "68:9/q05/p4", "position": "Stop attacking, taunting or harming the Prophet and allow his worship.", "reasons": "Bursevī and al-Kāshifī mention ending criticism; Ibn ʿĀshūr says they offered to stop calling him mad and leave each party to its worship. Asad and Kur'an Yolu say they promised to cease opposition or interference."}, {"id": "68:9/q05/p5", "position": "Dissemble or feign agreement in return.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās says they would feign agreement and dare sin; Zayd ibn Aslam calls it mutual hypocrisy; al-Ālūsī says their outward softness hides the opposite."}, {"id": "68:9/q05/p6", "position": "Lie too.", "reasons": "Al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas supplies this reciprocal gloss."}, {"id": "68:9/q05/p7", "position": "Weaken too.", "reasons": "Abū Jaʿfar supplies this reciprocal gloss."}, {"id": "68:9/q05/p8", "position": "Leave the mission along with him.", "reasons": "Qatāda's account says they would go along with his abandonment."}]}

{"id": "68:9/q08", "question": "What offers or events are reported behind this wish?", "turns_on": "Which reported proposal or related episode supplies the setting.", "positions": [{"id": "68:9/q08/p1", "position": "Quraysh polytheists invited the Prophet to their forefathers' religion or offered mutual noninterference.", "reasons": "Al-Jushumī reports the revelation setting; Ibn ʿĀshūr says sīra books place an offer through Abū Ṭālib and ʿUtba ibn Rabīʿa. {"id": "68:9/q09", "question": "What conduct does the verse require, and how does it distinguish courtesy from compromise?", "turns_on": "The motive and substance of the apparent softness: protection and reform, or surrender of religious truth for gain.", "positions": [{"id": "68:9/q09/p1", "position": "The Prophet must remain firm against religious or moral concessions to deniers.", "reasons": "Bursevī says he must persist despite their numbers and that obedience to a sinner or yielding to a tyrant is wrong; Elmalılı calls refusal a foundation of noble character; Kur'an Yolu says truth cannot be mixed with falsehood. Bursevī cites a Prophetic command to be courteous, al-Ghazālī on motive, and Abū al-Dardāʾ on smiling while inwardly condemning feared harm."}, {"id": "68:9/q09/p3", "position": "Words and outward action should agree with conviction.", "reasons": "Bursevī cites a Persian admonitory verse: words without deeds are false, a sleeper cannot awaken another, and counsel must be heard attentively; he warns that outward compliance without inner assent is hypocrisy."}]}
{"id": "68:9/q10", "question": "How does this wish connect with the surrounding command and opening of the sūra?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:9/q10/p1", "position": "It explains the command not to obey the deniers and answers their attacks on the Prophet.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the wish clause stands apart because it explains forbidden obedience; he connects their offer with accusations around 68:5–7 and 68:51. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says the opening affirms his mission against those calling the Qur'an ancient tales; Bursevī says he must keep confronting them."}]}
{"id": "68:9/q11", "question": "What motive or inward pattern does the wish reveal?", "turns_on": "Whether their desire reflects a wish to spread their own condition or self-interested bargaining.", "positions": [{"id": "68:9/q11/p1", "position": "Those who compromise want others to share their own condition.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī likens this to a sick person wishing others sick and says those marked by separation wish it on opponents; al-Biqāʿī repeats the analogy. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the fāʾ can explain their wish because people of bad intent seek others' likeness."}, {"id": "68:9/q11/p2", "position": "Their bargaining comes from desire rather than sincere religious conviction.", "reasons": "Islāhī says their opposition is bargaining against desire; Bursevī portrays them as steeped in vice and shifting desires, already flattering in hope of reciprocity."}]}
{"id": "68:42/q01", "question": "When is the day described? ", "turns_on": "Whether the summons requires a new legal obligation after death; others read it as rebuke.", "positions": [{"id": "68:42/q01/p1", "position": "The Day of Resurrection, especially its first or most severe hour.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id, al-Dahhak, Ibn Kathir, and the majority identify the final gathering; some describe the first hour or transition from earthly life. {"id": "68:42/q02", "question": "What governs the accusative time word yawm?", "turns_on": "The unstated governing word and whether this clause continues the earlier challenge.", "positions": [{"id": "68:42/q02/p1", "position": "It depends on the preceding challenge to bring alleged partners.", "reasons": "The partners are challenged to appear on that day to aid or intercede; al-Qurtubi says this forbids a pause at ṣādiqīn."}, {"id": "68:42/q02/p2", "position": "It depends on an implied imperative, 'remember' or 'mention.'", "reasons": "This starts a new sentence depicting the day's horrors; al-Qurtubi says a pause before yawm is then possible."}, {"id": "68:42/q02/p3", "position": "It depends on a suppressed event or predicate.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari and Razi say suppression heightens the threat; al-Samin also gives an omitted predicate."}, {"id": "68:42/q02/p4", "position": "It attaches to the later humbled-eyes or engulfing-shame clause.", "reasons": "Abu al-Baqa allows khāshiʿa but al-Samin finds it remote; Alusi and Elmalılı mention khāshiʿa or tarhaquhum."}]}
{"id": "68:42/q03", "question": "How is yukshafu read?", "turns_on": "The verbal subject and voice; the communal reading versus transmitted variants.", "positions": [{"id": "68:42/q03/p1", "position": "Passive third-person masculine yukshafu is the communal or majority reading.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas privileges the communal reading over soundly transmitted solitary variants; Ibn Atiyya, Ibn al-Jawzi, and Asim attest the raised yāʾ."}, {"id": "68:42/q03/p2", "position": "Active first-person plural nakshifu, 'We uncover.'", "reasons": "Reported from Ibn Abbas, Ibn Masud, Abu Mijlaz, Ibn Ya'mur, al-Dahhak and Ibn Hurmuz; it makes God the agent."}, {"id": "68:42/q03/p3", "position": "Active feminine takshifu: the Hour, Resurrection, or crisis uncovers.", "reasons": "Reported from Ibn Abbas, Ubayy, Hasan and others; al-Alusi finds the personification strained and its syntax problematic."}, {"id": "68:42/q03/p4", "position": "Passive feminine tukshafu with an understood feminine subject.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas is reported so; al-Samin says an implicit 'severity' is needed, while al-Alusi raises agreement objections."}, {"id": "68:42/q03/p5", "position": "Active masculine yakshifu with God as subject.", "reasons": "Reports attribute this to Ibn Masud, Ibn Abi Abla, Asim al-Jahdari and Abu al-Jawza; the verb has fatḥa on yāʾ and

 kasra on shīn."}, {"id": "68:42/q03/p6", "position": "A form from akshafa denotes entering a state of exposure.", "reasons": "Reported with tāʾ ḍamma and shīn kasra, or an intransitive yāʾ form; lexicographers compare the exposed lip of an akshaf man."}, {"id": "68:42/q03/p7", "position": "Ibn Kathir is reported to read the alif of sāq with hamza.", "reasons": "Ibn Khalawayh says all other readers agree on the alif form."}]}
{"id": "68:42/q04", "question": "What grammatical role and lexical range do the words about the sāq have?", "turns_on": "Whether the words are parsed literally, as a passive construction, or as a figurative phrase.", "positions": [{"id": "68:42/q04/p1", "position": "In the passive reading, ʿan sāq functions as the deputy subject.", "reasons": "Al-Samin and Bursevi state this iʿrāb; al-Alusi objects to some feminine alternatives because of gender agreement and preposition deletion."}, {"id": "68:42/q04/p2", "position": "Sāq is feminine and literally names a supporting leg, then a plant stem or trunk.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas notes its feminine diminutive takes tāʾ; Jishumi describes the animal limb supporting the body and a tree's trunk; Ibn al-Jawzi and Elmalılı give the literal and extended senses."}, {"id": "68:42/q04/p3", "position": "Kashf means removing a covering.", "reasons": "Jishumi gives the lexical sense; al-Rabi and Elmalılı apply it to lifting a veil."}]}
{"id": "68:42/q05", "question": "What is disclosed when a sāq is uncovered?", "turns_on": "Arabic idiom and poetry, transmitted divine-sign reports, and whether a literal divine body can be affirmed.", "positions": [{"id": "68:42/q05/p1", "position": "An immense crisis or the severity and terror of the Resurrection becomes manifest.", "reasons": "Arabic war, drought and hard-task idioms and many cited poems support the sense. Ibn Abbas urges seeking difficult Qur'anic language in poetry. Al-Tabari, al-Nahhas, al-Tabrisi, Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya, Razi, and Elmalılı favor this; some specify the first or hardest hour, afterlife's arrival, or accumulated horrors. The indefinite noun conveys unprecedented terror. Al-Nahhas also allows people literally baring their shins in distress; Tabatabai invokes work or flight and cites al-Kashshaf's miser analogy."}, {"id": "68:42/q05/p2", "position": "The foundation or underlying reality of the matter is laid bare, including deeds or hidden secrets.", "reasons": "Abu Sa'id al-Darir compares the supporting leg and tree trunk; Ibn Abbas says deeds appear. Ibn Mandah associates Ibn Masud's view with an active reading. Biqai says this need not conflict with severity."}, {"id": "68:42/q05/p5", "position": "The sāq belongs to the Throne.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayri reports this; Razi, Qurtubi and Elmalılı list it among unidentified possessors of the indefinite noun."}, {"id": "68:42/q05/p6", "position": "The sāq belongs to Hell.", "reasons": "Razi, Qurtubi and Elmalılı list this among possible referents."}, {"id": "68:42/q05/p7", "position": "The sāq belongs to an awe-inspiring angel.", "reasons": "Razi and Elmalılı list this proposal; the wording does not name its possessor."}, {"id": "68:42/q05/p8", "position": "God Himself becomes manifest, with sāq understood as 'self.'", "reasons": "Abu Umar al-Zahid adduces Ali's use of sāq for self; Elmalılı describes divine truth and judgment appearing from the unseen, without specifying modality."}, {"id": "68:42/q05/p9", "position": "A veil is lifted.", "reasons": "Al-Rabi speaks of a veil lifted; Abu Musa's fuller report connects it with divine recognition and prostration."}]}
{"id": "68:42/q06", "question": "What image gives the idiom its force?", "turns_on": "Different accounts of the concrete scene behind the established figurative usage.", "positions": [{"id": "68:42/q06/p1", "position": "Someone facing hard work bares the shin or gathers up clothing to exert effort.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, Thalabi, Ibn Atiyya, Abu Ubayda, Qurtubi and others cite Duraid, Hudhali, war and drought verse. Jishumi notes repeated use made the image proverbial; Elmalılı includes readiness and urgency."}, {"id": "68:42/q06/p2", "position": "Panicked people, especially modest women fleeing defeat, lift their garments and expose their legs.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari, Baydawi, Alusi, Bursevi, Ibn Ashur and Islahi explain this scene; Ibn Qays al-Ruqayyat's poem and Anas's Uhud account illustrate exposed legs under urgent conditions."}, {"id": "68:42/q06/p3", "position": "The idiom derives from the difficult extraction of a camel calf.", "reasons": "Abu Muslim invokes the mudhammir helper, birth omens, and verses of al-Kumayt and another poet."}]}
{"id": "68:42/q07", "question": "What does the indefinite sāq contribute?", "turns_on": "Whether indefiniteness marks an extraordinary crisis, disallows a specified limb, or exalts a revealed foundation.", "positions": [{"id": "68:42/q07/p1", "position": "It magnifies an unfamiliar, unprecedented terror.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari compares the unknown terror of 54:6; Baydawi, Abu Hayyan, Bursevi, Alusi and Elmalılı stress awe or magnitude."}, {"id": "68:42/q07/p2", "position": "It is not possessively specified, weakening identification with a familiar divine limb.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari, Razi, Nasafi and Elmalılı use the indefinite form against a corporeal referent; Razi asks how an uncovered leg would identify God."}, {"id": "68:42/q07/p3", "position": "On the foundation reading, it conveys exaltation.", "reasons": "Bursevi and Alusi mention this alternative, while Alusi notes that a parabolic image need not be parsed word by word."}]}
{"id": "68:42/q08", "question": "How do commentators treat a bodily reading of God's sāq?", "turns_on": "The force of divine possessive reports, corporeality proofs, Arabic figurative usage, and treatment of ambiguous attributes.", "positions": [{"id": "68:42/q08/p1", "position": "A literal divine bodily limb is rejected; the expression is read figuratively or its modality left to God.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi and Qurtubi deny parts or cover; Razi argues bodies are finite, originated and contingent; Zamakhshari and Nasafi cite rhetoric and the indefinite noun. Razi insists figurative interpretation needs decisive proof, warning from 2:25 and 22:77 against unrestricted metaphor."}, {"id": "68:42/q08/p2", "position": "The wording and transmitted reports are accepted as an ambiguous divine attribute or imaginal manifestation.", "reasons": "Some exegetes and the Salaf leave the report among ambiguous texts; esoteric Sufis take the visual manifestation in an imaginal mode. Abu Ubayda, quoted by Zamakhshari, portrays Muqatil and Jahm as opposing extremes."}]}
{"id": "68:42/q09", "question": "What sequence do the reports place around the disclosure?", "turns_on": "The transmitted scene and its variants, plus the reliability assigned to particular transmissions.", "positions": [{"id": "68:42/q09/p1", "position": "After a long gathering, communities follow their claimed objects of worship; monotheists await and recognize God at the sign, then sincere believers prostrate while hypocrites fail.", "reasons": "Ibn Masud reports forty years standing; Abu Hurayra describes settled wrongs, likenesses of Ezra and Jesus, and light and bridge crossing; Abu Sa'id compares vision to sun and moon. Variants add Paradise, Fire, intercession, and different speeds across the bridge."}, {"id": "68:42/q09/p2", "position": "The unveiling is a great light at which people fall in prostration.", "reasons": "Abu Musa transmits this wording; al-Bayhaqi grades the report weak and Ibn Kathir notes an unidentified transmitter."}, {"id": "68:42/q09/p3", "position": "The disclosure is the lifting of a veil.", "reasons": "Al-Rabi reports this; the Abu Musa scene says the monotheists recognize God when the veil lifts."}, {"id": "68:42/q09/p4", "position": "The reports differ in detail and are assessed differently.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya notes additions and omissions. {"id": "68:42/q11", "question": "Who issues or conveys the summons?", "turns_on": "Whether the passive leaves a divine, angelic, human, visual, or inward caller implied.", "positions": [{"id": "68:42/q11/p1", "position": "God calls them, directly or through an angel.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi says the apparent caller is God or an angel; Ibn Ashur suggests angels assigned to the gathering, citing 54:6–8. {"id": "68:42/q12", "question": "Why are they called to prostrate?", "turns_on": "Whether the scene is a post-resurrection test and rebuke, a legal command, an attempt at rescue, or worldly prayer.", "positions": [{"id": "68:42/q12/p1", "position": "The summons is rebuke and humiliation for refusing prostration while able in earthly life.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas, Jishumi, Razi, Nasafi, Biqai, Bursevi and others deny a new legal duty in the afterlife. {"id": "68:42/q13", "question": "Why can they not prostrate?", "turns_on": "Whether inability is bodily punishment, removed capacity, missed opportunity, or an exposed inner disposition.", "positions": [{"id": "68:42/q13/p1", "position": "Their backs or limbs become a single rigid bone, plate, horn, or skewer, so they cannot bend and may fall backward.", "reasons": "Ibn Masud, Ibn Abbas, Muqatil and Prophetic reports give these physical images; Biqai calls the hadith authentic. Variations describe one vertebra, cattle horns, spits, and a flat board; Wahidi says the failure follows neglect or ostentation in life."}, {"id": "68:42/q13/p2", "position": "God removes their effective capacity at that moment.", "reasons": "Razi, Abu Hayyan, Alusi and Ibn Ashur state that ability is withheld as punishment, intensifying grief; Biqai emphasizes their still wanting to submit."}, {"id": "68:42/q13/p3", "position": "The useful time for prostration and deeds has passed.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas, Ibn Bahr, Tabrisi and Baydawi say an afterlife prostration cannot make up earthly neglect; on the death reading the patient cannot rise."}, {"id": "68:42/q13/p4", "position": "Their ingrained arrogance or dark inner dispositions prevent inward submission.", "reasons": "Tabatabai says arrogance became fixed and hidden reality is exposed, citing 86:9; Qashani blames bodily veils that destroyed original readiness."}, {"id": "68:42/q13/p5", "position": "They lacked sincere worldly worship and are exposed by the test.", "reasons": "Abu Sa'id contrasts willing worship with fear or show; Wahidi says unbelievers had never prostrated; Biqai says people rise in the state in which they died."}]}
{"id": "68:42/q14", "question": "What theological inference is drawn from their inability?", "turns_on": "Whether later inability proves earlier capacity and whether an impossible assignment is admissible.", "positions": [{"id": "68:42/q14/p1", "position": "Their later inability implies that disbelievers possessed worldly capacity to believe.", "reasons": "Al-Jubbai argues that specifying inability in the Hereafter implies its absence was not true in worldly life."}, {"id": "68:42/q14/p2", "position": "That inference fails; capacity accompanies the act rather than preceding it.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya invokes Ash'ari doctrine; Razi replies using divine foreknowledge, and Abu Hayyan denies the temporal inference."}, {"id": "68:42/q14/p3", "position": "A task beyond one's capacity may be assigned, though no intrinsically irrational task can.", "reasons": "Bursevi reports Ash'ari permission and Mu'tazili prohibition, and says no one permits ordering the annihilation of the eternal."}]}
{"id": "68:42/q15", "question": "How does the verse connect with the surrounding passage?", "turns_on": "The transition from the partners challenge, the contrast with verse 43, and the sūra's wider symbolism.", "positions": [{"id": "68:42/q15/p1", "position": "It brings the challenge to alleged partners into Judgment, where their claim to help or intercede fails.", "reasons": "Zajjaj, Wahidi, Razi, Ibn Ashur, Tabatabai and Islahi connect the preceding challenge and claimed felicity to exposure at the gathering; Elmalılı reads warning for criminals and glad tidings for believers."}, {"id": "68:42/q15/p2", "position": "The contrast with being called while safe explains why they cannot respond now.", "reasons": "Biqai finds iḥtibāk: inability here implies former ability, and former safety implies present unsafety. Study Quran distinguishes Judgment's prostration from the worldly call in verse 43."}, {"id": "68:42/q15/p3", "position": "The unveiling distinguishes outward prostration from inward devotion.", "reasons": "Biqai says visible prostration expresses submission and the devotion within; Elmalılı links it to the manifestation of truth and judgment."}, {"id": "68:42/q15/p4", "position": "The imagery gives a symbolic echo of the sūra's opening nūn.", "reasons": "Elmalılı makes this comparison."}]}
{"id": "68:42/q16", "question": "What inward reading is given?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:42/q16/p1", "position": "The terrifying unveiled ordeal and spiritual summons reveal how mercy, justice, and prior inward habits determine response.", "reasons": "Ja'far says divine care spares a believer the Bridge and Judgment terrors, while one met by justice has a stone-like back; one saint's meeting another unveils hardships. {"id": "68:42/q17", "question": "How do broader linguistic notes illuminate this figurative expression?", "turns_on": "How general Arabic rhetoric and grammar bear on reading the verse's compact image.", "positions": [{"id": "68:42/q17/p1", "position": "Arabic transfers words by association, resemblance, and context, and figures can be stronger than direct wording.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba offers rain called sky, vegetation anwa', earth or clouds 'laughing,' and hardship as 'sweat'; Jurjani separates lexical transfer from agency attribution, describes representation, sensory simile and degrees of metaphor; Zarkashi compares apt 'wing of humility' with dubious 'water of blame' and cites war uncovering a shin. Razi says metaphor needs proof before displacing a literal scriptural sense."}, {"id": "68:42/q17/p2", "position": "The Qur'an's language requires careful eloquence, without treating any element as meaningless surplus.", "reasons": "Baqqillani contrasts its inimitability with Imru al-Qays and ordinary saj', and rejects proposed weaknesses of Qur'anic variation; Kashshaf demands semantic and rhetorical expertise; Zarkashi and Suyuti describe the caution and skills needed for ambiguous passages."}, {"id": "68:42/q17/p3", "position": "Arabic vocative particles can mark distance, emphasis, or direct presence and are sometimes omitted.", "reasons": "Sibawayh's five forms and the rare poetic omission of ya show that expression depends on context; his examples include lamentation and imploring."}]}

{"id": "68:43/q01", "question": "What is the state of their eyes?", "turns_on": "Whether the description is outward abasement or an inward loss of perception.", "positions": [{"id": "68:43/q01/p1", "position": "Their gaze is downcast, humbled and unable to lift in shame or fear.", "reasons": "Muqātil and al-Wāḥidī link it to seeing the Fire and becoming sure of punishment; al-Jishumī adds fearful expectation; al-Kāshifī describes bowed heads; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it a transfer from the posture of an abased person. {"id": "68:43/q04", "question": "What does تَرْهَقُهُمْ mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:43/q04/p1", "position": "It reaches, covers, overtakes or overwhelms them.", "reasons": "Bursawī explains rahq as one thing covering another; Ibn ʿĀshūr adds eager approach and compares 80:41. {"id": "68:43/q05", "question": "What is the humiliation that overtakes them?", "turns_on": "Whether the disgrace is described as outward shame, remorse, punishment, or inward attachment.", "positions": [{"id": "68:43/q05/p1", "position": "It is severe, visible disgrace and abasement.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī says their submission becomes visible; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the soul's humiliation appears externally; Bursawī derives it from the root and dhalīl; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī stresses that it is coercive."}, {"id": "68:43/q05/p2", "position": "It is the shame of regret and grief at their refusal and inability.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās identifies remorse; al-Rāzī likens them to a servant abandoned and shamed by his master; al-Biqāʿī traces shame to limbs spent on pleasures away from God; Ibn Kathīr calls it reversal of worldly arrogance."}, {"id": "68:43/q05/p3", "position": "It comes from God's punishment when they see the Fire.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī names divine punishment; Muqātil and al-Wāḥidī say their eyes lower on seeing the Fire or certainty of punishment."}, {"id": "68:43/q05/p4", "position": "It is inward attachment to lower things and bodily nature.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī describes stagnation in inferior passive states."}]}
{"id": "68:43/q06", "question": "How is تَرْهَقُهُمْ ذِلَّةٌۭ related syntactically to the preceding description?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause is circumstantial or independent.", "positions": [{"id": "68:43/q06/p1", "position": "It is a second circumstantial clause describing those unable or summoned.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās allows an accusative circumstantial clause; Ibn ʿĀshūr attaches it to the pronoun in 'they are unable'; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī counts two circumstantial clauses."}, {"id": "68:43/q06/p2", "position": "It can be detached from the preceding clause.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās gives this alternative."}]}
{"id": "68:43/q07", "question": "What happens to believers' and nonbelievers' faces after the prostration?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:43/q07/p1", "position": "Believers' faces shine white or bright; hypocrites' and disbelievers' faces blacken.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī and al-Qurṭubī say whiter than snow and darker than pitch; al-Biqāʿī says brighter than the sun; Abū al-Layth includes Jews and Christians among those grieving with dark faces."}]}
{"id": "68:43/q08", "question": "Whom does the failed prostration expose?", "turns_on": "Whether the failed test is aimed at hidden hypocrisy, open disbelief, or insincere worship.", "positions": [{"id": "68:43/q08/p1", "position": "It exposes hypocrites who stood among Muslims.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr explicitly prefers the allusion to hypocrites; reports repeatedly contrast true believers with hypocrites whose backs stiffen. Al-Qurṭubī says this report pattern is established in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim through Abū Saʿīd and others."}, {"id": "68:43/q08/p2", "position": "It also includes unbelievers or polytheists who rejected God's summons.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās names unbelievers; Ibn Kathīr and the Turkish commentary name both disbelievers and hypocrites; al-Shawkānī's narration says even unbelievers wish to prostrate."}, {"id": "68:43/q08/p3", "position": "It includes people whose worldly prostrations were ostentatious or fearful.", "reasons": "Abū Saʿīd's Prophetic report contrasts willing, sincere prostration with fear or display; the Turkish commentary reports the ostentatious men and women cannot bend."}]}
{"id": "68:43/q09", "question": "What scene unfolds when people are summoned to prostrate on Judgment Day?", "turns_on": "The reports vary in sequence, forty-year duration, accompanying signs, final destinations and named groups.", "positions": [{"id": "68:43/q09/p1", "position": "True worshippers recognize God at the disclosure and prostrate; hypocrites try but cannot.", "reasons": "Abū Saʿīd, Abū Hurayra, Ibn Masʿūd, Qatāda, and other transmitted accounts give the shared contrast; backs become rigid, flat, fused, or one bone. Al-Qurṭubī says its meaning occurs in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim; al-Dāraquṭnī and al-Ḥākim grade the Ibn Masʿūd account sound."}, {"id": "68:43/q09/p2", "position": "After forty years of standing, worshippers follow false gods to Hell; sincere Muslims prostrate and hypocrites are sent to Hell.", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿūd and ʿAbdallāh report the forty years; al-Ṭabarī's accounts mention believers then enter Paradise and receive rewards; al-Thaʿlabī's version says the gathering is barefoot and naked; al-Qurṭubī's version includes a declaration of divine justice and compares 83:6."}, {"id": "68:43/q09/p3", "position": "After other worshippers are led away, believers recognize God by a sign; hypocrites fall backward, and survivors cross a bridge by varying lights.", "reasons": "Abū Hurayra names angels resembling ʿUzayr and Jesus and a prior settling of wrongs; his other report describes bridge speeds. Ibn Masʿūd's report says light varies by deeds and may flicker at the feet."}, {"id": "68:43/q09/p4", "position": "Idol worshippers, Jews and Christians are separated before the remaining worshippers meet their Lord.", "reasons": "Abū Saʿīd's accounts say other groups follow their objects of worship; one al-Ṭabarī transmission merely recalls the coming described before; al-Ḥasan's report says Muslims remain to be tested."}, {"id": "68:43/q09/p5", "position": "In Abū Mūsā's account, monotheists recognize the Lord when the veil lifts, and each is replaced by a Jew or Christian in Hell.", "reasons": "Abū Bardah swore three times his father transmitted it; ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz liked no report about monotheists more. Al-Qurṭubī states no grading there."}, {"id": "68:43/q09/p6", "position": "Qatāda's account describes the unveiling as a horrendous event in which believers' prostration rebukes hypocrites.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī also transmits a Prophetic form of the report; the specific stress is humiliation brought by believers' act."}]}
